hints: Recall the two quark charge families: up-type quarks (u, c) have charge $+\frac{2}{3}e$ and down-type quarks (d, s, b) have charge $-\frac{1}{3}e$.
Apply the antimatter rule that an antiquark has opposite sign but same magnitude of charge as its quark: $Q_{\bar{q}} = -Q_{q}$.
teacher_walkthrough: Quark charge is quantised in fractions of $e$: up-type $Q = +\frac{2}{3}e$, down-type $Q = -\frac{1}{3}e$.
Therefore $Q_d = -\frac{1}{3}e$ and $Q_c = +\frac{2}{3}e$ because c is up-type like u.
walkthrough: B1: d quark charge $-1/3e$ and c quark charge $+2/3e$.
B1: all three antiquark charges opposite to quarks: anti-u $-2/3e$, anti-d $+1/3e$, anti-c $-2/3e$.
common_pitfalls: Giving antiquarks the same charge as quarks instead of reversing the sign.
Swapping the families by giving d $+2/3e$ and c $-1/3e$.
Writing charges as decimals or in coulombs instead of units of $e$ as required by the charge/e column.

hints: A baryon contains three quarks and total charge must sum to zero: select $u$ and $d$ quarks whose fractional charges cancel.
teacher_walkthrough: Baryon rule: a baryon is $qqq$ with total charge $$Q = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3$$
Combine: $$Q/e = \frac{2-1-1}{3} = \frac{0}{3} = 0$$ so $udd$ is neutral and valid.
walkthrough: B1: state $udd$ in any order (udd, dud, ddu) as a neutral baryon.
common_pitfalls: Using an antiquark symbol, which would make a pentaquark or other exotic state, not a baryon.
Stating $uuu$ or $ddd$ which give charges $+2e$ and $-e$ respectively, not zero.

hints: A meson is one quark plus one antiquark: pick a pair whose charges add to $+1e$, e.g. a $+2/3$ quark with a $+1/3$ antiquark.
teacher_walkthrough: Meson rule: a meson is $q\bar{q}$ with total charge $$Q = Q_q + Q_{\bar{q}}$$
Add: $$Q/e = \frac{2+1}{3} = \frac{3}{3} = +1$$ so charge is $+e$ as required.
walkthrough: B1: state $u\bar{d}$ as a meson with charge $+e$.
common_pitfalls: Stating two quarks e.g. $ud$, which is not a meson structure.
Stating $d\bar{u}$ which gives $-1/3 + (-2/3) = -1$, i.e. charge $-e$ not $+e$.

hints: Recall the Standard Model divides fundamental matter particles into two classes: quarks and the class containing the electron.
teacher_walkthrough: Fundamental matter in the Standard Model is divided into quarks and leptons.
Electrons carry no colour charge and do not interact via the strong force, which defines them as leptons.
walkthrough: B1: name the group as leptons.
common_pitfalls: Answering hadrons or baryons, which are composite particles made of quarks, not fundamental.
Answering mesons or bosons, confusing force carriers with matter particles.

hints: Recall other members of the electron family: the heavier charged versions or the neutral partners produced in beta decay.
teacher_walkthrough:
Lepton family contains six flavours: $e$, $\mu$, $	au$ and their neutrinos $
u_e$, $
u_\mu$, $
u_	au$.
Any one other than the electron is acceptable, e.g. muon or electron neutrino.
walkthrough: B1: state muon or tau or any neutrino (electron neutrino, muon neutrino, tau neutrino).
common_pitfalls: Stating a quark e.g. up or down, which is in the other fundamental group.
Stating proton or neutron, which are baryons and not fundamental.
